analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import lower-priced prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the 115th Congress, dying after being referred to the Senate Health Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules, within 185 days, allowing individuals to buy prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies and import up to a 90-day supply for personal use. Only drugs identical to FDA-approved ones would qualify, and controlled substances, biologics, and certain other drug types would be excluded. The goal is to let Americans pay Canadian prices for the same medicines.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs, especially those without insurance or with high deductibles. Canadian drug prices are often far lower than U.S. prices for the same medicines, so personal importation would let some patients cut their out-of-pocket drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to issue regulations within 185 days permitting individuals to import a prescription drug purchased from an approved Canadian pharmacy, in quantities of up to a 90-day supply for personal use [S2][S3].

Imported drugs must have the same active ingredients, route of administration, dosage form, and strength as an FDA-approved drug, and be dispensed by a pharmacist licensed in Canada under a valid U.S. prescription [S2][S3].

The bill sets up a certification process for Canadian pharmacies — requiring at least 5 years in operation, provincial compliance, quality assurance and lab testing — and requires HHS to publish a list of approved pharmacies on the FDA website [S2][S3].
Higher-risk products are excluded: controlled substances, biological products, infused and intravenously injected drugs, refrigerated drugs, and others [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose ability to keep U.S. prices well above Canadian prices depends on blocking parallel imports. To the extent importation reduces their U.S. sales at high margins, some revenue pressure could also fall on drug research budgets.

drawbacks.text: Safety is the core objection: the FDA has long argued that drugs sold abroad, even in Canada, cannot always be verified to U.S. standards, and counterfeit or mislabeled products could slip through the mail — which is why the bill excludes biologics, controlled substances, and refrigerated drugs [S2][S3].

The bill is narrow by design: it covers only personal importation of up to a 90-day supply, so it would not lower prices across the whole market or address the underlying gap between U.S. and Canadian drug prices [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing high out-of-pocket drug costs, the benefit is direct and immediate — the same medicine at Canadian prices. The safety risk is real but the bill addresses it with strict certification, testing, and exclusions of the highest-risk drug categories. The bigger limitation is scope: personal importation helps individuals who use it, but it is a small lever compared with the overall U.S.-Canada price gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) introduced the bill on January 10, 2017, with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1][S3][S5].
It drew 10 cosponsors — 8 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent [S4].
No further action was taken after the committee referral; the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept the current system in which U.S. patients pay higher prices than Canadians for the same drugs. Consumers who might have used importation gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to allow personal drug importation from Canada.

for.name: 8 Democratic senators, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; no markup or vote was scheduled in two years.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Long campaigned against prescription drug importation, arguing it would undermine drug safety and U.S. pricing, and its opposition has been cited in the defeat of similar importation bills for decades.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring any version of drug importation to the Senate floor during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor plus 10 cosponsors split 8 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — but no vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call record of the split [S4][S5].

industries.note: Importation would let Americans buy identical drugs at Canadian prices, cutting into U.S. sales priced far higher. The industry has historically opposed importation bills to preserve the U.S. price structure.
Certified pharmacies that meet the bill's standards would gain legal access to American customers buying 90-day supplies.
Patients who import drugs would bypass some U.S. retail pharmacies and intermediaries, though the bill's 90-day personal-use limit keeps the effect small.
